implementation_notes: C has no classes or virtual dispatch, so the classic structure is written by hand: the component interface is a struct whose first member is a function-pointer table, and the C guarantee that a pointer to a struct can be cast to a pointer to its first member is what lets a `Reader *` be passed where the wrapper's own layout is expected. Every decorator embeds the interface struct as its first member, holds a pointer to the wrapped component, and fills the function entries with its own functions that call inward before or after doing their work; ownership travels with the wrapper, so the close/free entry is part of the interface and releases the chain from the outside in. There is no simpler local replacement - this structure is the price of a genuine responsibility pipeline in C, and embedded code often pays it without malloc by statically initialising the wrappers.
idiom_name: struct with a function-pointer table; wrapper embeds the interface struct as its first member and holds the inner pointer
pitfalls: The interface struct must be the first member of every concrete type and every decorator; the cast to the wrapper is only valid under that layout, and a reordered struct corrupts the chain at runtime.

Ownership is manual: the wrapper owns the object it wraps, so freeing both the outer and the inner pointer double-frees - the close entry must release inward and callers must drop their inner references.
Nothing checks that a wrapper forwards every interface entry: a decorator that omits one silently drops behaviour for every layer beneath it, and the compiler stays silent.
